description: The UCSF Management of the Hospitalized Patient course, chaired by Bob Wachter, MD, is the longest-running and most popular CME course for hospitalists and others who care for hospitalized patients. Taught by UCSF’s top teachers, including Gurpreet Dhaliwal, S. Andrew Josephson, Lekshmi Santhosh, Tracy Minichiello, and Bradley Sharpe, the course highlights recent evidence and current controversies, and blends lectures with multiple interactive workshops to promote active learning. Content areas include critical care, perioperative care, hospital neurology, infectious diseases, cardiology, and nephrology, as well as AI, diagnostic reasoning, and management of the patient with substance use disorder. All of this at the beautiful Hyatt Embarcadero in the heart of San Francisco’s waterfront district. This course is presented by the UCSF Division of Hospital Medicine and is sponsored by the Office of Continuing Medical Education, University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine. It also serves as the West Coast regional meeting of the Society of Hospital Medicine.

description: Linking Biomarkers to Lived Use: Concordance Between Serum and Urine Drug Biomarker Concentrations and Self-Reported Opioid Use Among a Prospective Cohort of Individuals Using Opioids in San Francisco John Halifax, MS • Graduate Student Researcher • Division of Epidemiology • UC Berkeley School of Public Health In this upcoming talk, John Halifax will present findings from the San Francisco General Hospital Opioid Treatment Outpatient Program’s (OTOP) toxicology monitoring program and the OCTUPUS (Optimizing Comprehensive drug Testing for Overdose Prevention Using Substance use biomarkers) study of reported “iso” use in San Francisco. In early 2023, patients at SFGH began reporting use of “tranq” and “iso,” thought to refer to fentanyl mixed with xylazine and the synthetic opioid isotonitazene, respectively. In response, OTOP launched urine toxicology monitoring in March 2023 to provide timely data to patients, clinicians, and public health leaders. The OCTUPUS study further surveyed a subset of OTOP intake patients about recent substance use and linked their reports with expanded toxicology testing. This talk will review findings from OTOP monitoring and examine OCTUPUS data to clarify the meaning and clinical significance of reported “iso” use. John Halifax is an Epidemiology PhD student at UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health. He broadly explores the role of neighborhood and place as determinants of health from an ecosocial perspective using flexible, minimally assumptive causal inference methods. His current research includes extending causal inference methods to account for neighborhood-specific confounding effects in multilevel, high-dimensional data settings, examining the effect of acute community violence on perinatal outcomes, and utilizing machine learning to forecast fatal overdoses at the neighborhood level. Prior to pursuing a PhD, John worked at the intersection of analytical chemistry, community health, and the overdose crisis at San Francisco AIDS Foundation and UC San Francisco. John holds an MS in Epidemiology from UC Berkeley and a BS in Chemistry magna cum laude from Haverford College. Outside of work, you will find John riding his bicycle, cooking heirloom beans, or watching his favorite soccer team lose again. --------------------------------- The UCSF Drug Use Research Group (DURG) is a city-wide seminar attended by faculty, postdoctoral fellows, graduate students, and other Bay Area investigators centering on persons who use drugs. The DURG was founded in 2005 after a friendly debate between an epidemiologist and anthropologist on the merits of quantitative versus qualitative research methods. These monthly meetings provide a community platform for new and established investigators to present their works-in-progress, consult on new or related research and policy questions, and prepare for grant applications, conferences, and publications in a supportive environment. The seminar has been successful in cultivating new research collaborations, mentorship, and sustaining interdisciplinary and interprofessional dialogue between those engaged in basic sciences, epidemiology, clinical research, and qualitative methods. Our meetings are not recorded or live-streamed. If you would like to attend the seminar or present your work for dissemination, collaboration, and/or peer review, please contact Leslie Suen, MD, MAS: Leslie.Suen@ucsf.edu

description: Join UCSF researchers for a practical look at new generative AI models, tools, platforms and workflows designed to facilitate and expedite scientific research! Title: "Benchmarking Automated Scientific Enquiry: When AI co-scientists outpace peer review, what becomes the arbiter of truth?" Featured Speaker: Luca Foschini, PhD President & CEO, Sage Bionetworks Seminar 3-4pm, Networking Reception 4-5pm Share the Flyer! Bio: Luca Foschini, PhD, is President and CEO of Sage Bionetworks, a nonprofit that builds open infrastructure for biomedical data sharing, including the Synapse platform and community challenges such as DREAM. Before Sage he co-founded Evidation Health, where as Chief Data Scientist he spent over a decade leading research on wearable and real-world data for health. He holds a PhD in Computer Science from UC Santa Barbara, has published more than 70 peer-reviewed papers, and in a previous life represented Italy at the International Olympiad in Informatics. Abstract: In under two years, AI systems went from grade-school math to research-level problems, and the length of tasks an agent can complete reliably keeps doubling every few months. More than twenty AI co-scientists now promise to search the literature, generate hypotheses, analyze data and write up results. Do they reason like scientists? Recent evidence says not yet: agents often gather evidence and then ignore it, and better scaffolds barely help. The deeper problem is verification. AI moves fastest where answers can be checked instantly, as in code or proofs, while biology checks its claims at the pace of the wet lab and of peer review. I will walk through what works today, where these tools fail, and how benchmarks run as living community efforts, kept fresh and re-run on every new model, can keep us honest about what is still true., powered by Localist, the Community Event Platform
